title: Twin XOR
statement: A security team pairs sensor IDs so their bitwise XOR is as large as possible, to make collisions unlikely. Given non-negative integers in values, return the largest value of values[i] XOR values[j] over all pairs with i < j.

hints.content: XOR is maximized by making the highest possible bit 1, then the next, and so on (a greedy choice from the top bit).
For a given value, you want a partner whose bit differs at each position, starting from the highest.
Store the values seen so far in a binary trie keyed by bits from 30 down to 0.
For each new value, walk the trie preferring the opposite bit at every level; that path spells its best partner. Insert the value afterwards.

testCases.explanation: 10 XOR 2 is 8, but 8 XOR 2 = 10 is larger.
A mixed list where 36 XOR 91 = 127 is best.
Many large values: checking every pair is too slow.

solutions.title: Try every pair
solutions.intuition: Compute XOR for each pair and keep the maximum.
solutions.approach: Two nested loops over i < j.
solutions.pseudocode: best = 0; for i < j: best = max(best, v[i] ^ v[j]); return best
commonMistakes: Using a signed shift or values above 2^31 - 1, which makes ^ return negative numbers in JavaScript.
solutions.interviewExplanation: The pairwise scan is the baseline, at about 50 million XORs for 10,000 values.

solutions.title: Greedy walk in a binary trie
solutions.intuition: Choosing the opposite bit as high up as possible maximizes XOR, and a trie of earlier values tells you instantly whether that opposite bit is available.
solutions.approach: Represent the trie with two child arrays (zero and one). Insert the first value. For each next value, walk from bit 30 to 0: if the opposite child exists, take it and set that bit in the result; otherwise follow the same bit. Update the answer, then insert the value.
solutions.pseudocode:
insert(v[0]); best = 0
for v in rest: node = root; x = 0
  for bit 30..0: want = 1 - bit(v); if child[want]: x |= 1 << bit; go want else go other
  best = max(best, x); insert(v)
commonMistakes: Querying before inserting anything, which walks an empty trie.
Using 1 << 31, which is negative in JavaScript; 31 bits (30..0) suffice here.
solutions.interviewExplanation: XOR is maximized greedily from the top bit, so for each value I walk a binary trie of earlier values, taking the opposite bit whenever it exists. Each insert and query is 31 steps, so it's O(31n). An alternative builds the answer bit by bit with a hash set of prefixes, also O(31n).

steps.title: Step 1
steps.content: Insert 3, 10 and 5. For 25 (11001): want 0 at bit 4. 5 = 00101 is there, so the path follows 5.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: The result is 25 ^ 5 = 28; later values do not beat it.
